conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for coming in today. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. First, let me say how normal it is to feel a little uncertain or overwhelmed in the weeks after having a baby; you’re not alone in that.

Because mood changes are so common after childbirth, I’d like to spend a few minutes with you on a short questionnaire called the EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. Everything you share is confidential, and this space is completely judgment-free—my goal is simply to understand how best to support you right now.

We’ll go through ten gentle questions. Please answer in whatever words feel natural; there are no right or wrong responses. If at any point something feels difficult to talk about, just let me know and we can pause or adjust.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

Honestly... I’ve laughed maybe a couple of times, but only if my husband or my mom made a joke right in front of me. Most of the day it just feels like my sense of humor is buried under this heavy blanket—like even if something is funny, it barely reaches me. I’ll smile for a second and then go right back to feeling flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wish I could say that. I mean, I can force a little chuckle when my husband is being goofy with the baby, but it doesn’t feel natural or last more than a second. Most of the time nothing feels funny—just kind of gray.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake, even just a quiet shower. Now… it’s like I remember I liked those things, but when I think about doing them, I feel nothing. I still go, because I hope it’ll help, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that one hits. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong.” I keep replaying every little choice—did I eat the wrong thing, hold him too much, not enough? Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still feel like I’m failing somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind keeps circling around scary “what-ifs” about the baby—like what if he stops breathing in the night or what if I drop him. I know the chances are tiny, but I can’t turn the thoughts off. They just spin until I feel tight in my chest.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week it’s felt like an alarm going off in my body—heart racing, can’t catch my breath, palms sweaty. There’s no real danger; I’ll just be folding laundry and suddenly feel like something awful is about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. It’s like the dishes, the laundry, feeding him every two hours, trying to sleep in between—everything piles up, and I feel I’m drowning in it. Some mornings I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, not knowing where to start, and the knot in my stomach keeps tightening.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I dread bedtime. I lie there exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—mostly worries about the baby and whether I’m cut out for this. It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and then I wake up every couple of hours with my heart pounding, sure I heard him cry even when he’s still asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… sad feels like the baseline now. I’m not crying all day, but there’s this heavy, gray cloud that just sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears in my eyes, or I’ll look at him sleeping and think, “I should be feeling so happy,” and instead I just feel empty.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried twice this week. Once was after my mom left—she’d been helping all day, and when she walked out the door I just felt this wave of “I can’t do this alone,” and the tears came. The other time was at 3 a.m.; the baby wouldn’t settle, I couldn’t get him latched, and I just sat in the rocker sobbing while he cried, too.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I’ve had a couple of quick flashes—like “what if I just kept driving past the house and never came back,” or a picture of cutting myself with the kitchen knife—but they’re gone in a second. I don’t want to die and I don’t have a plan; it’s more like my brain is testing how bad things could get. Still, it scares me that those thoughts pop in at all.

You've shared that the joy and spark you once felt have been replaced by a heavy, gray mood that makes even small pleasures feel out of reach. Daily tasks feel overwhelming, your mind races with worries about your baby, and you've been startled by brief flashes of self-harm thoughts that leave you frightened. Yet you're still showing up-feeding, comforting, and caring for your little one-while feeling exhausted, tearful, and convinced you're failing.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to experience natural laughter, describes mood as "gray," and only forces brief chuckles—matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure—she feels "nothing" when thinking of activities she once enjoyed</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly reports frequent, pervasive self-blame and feelings of failure, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Daily intrusive catastrophic worries about the baby with physical tension map to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Classic description of panic attacks occurring several times in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to start tasks, and physically tense—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes severe, persistent sleep disruption tied to unhappiness—taking over an hour to fall asleep, frequent night waking, and racing thoughts—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness as baseline, unexpected tearfulness, and emotional emptiness despite positive moments</sym>, <sym>Patient describes fleeting but recurrent intrusive self-harm images (driving past home, cutting) that occur "sometimes" without intent or plan, matching "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score of 26 (≥14) indicates probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset, reinforced by daily anhedonia, marked self-blame, multiple panic-type episodes, sleep disruption, and passive self-harm thoughts (<quote>quick flashes… picture of cutting myself</quote>). Pattern meets <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call local 24/7 crisis line or 988 if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Ask your provider about evidence-based treatments for <med>postpartum depression</med> including <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and possible <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
4. Enlist partner or family to handle one night feeding so you can obtain a 4-5 hour stretch of sleep; practice short 10-minute daytime rest periods when baby naps
5. Schedule brief daily outdoor walks with baby in carrier or stroller-morning sunlight can help regulate mood and sleep
6. Reduce task load: leave dishes in sink, order grocery delivery, accept all offered help; focus only on baby care and personal recovery
7. Begin simple breathing exercise: inhale 4 s, hold 4 s, exhale 6 s, repeat 5 times when panic sensations start; consider free perinatal anxiety apps for guided support
8. Attend local <med>mothers' support group</med> or virtual <med>PMAD support circle</med>; peer contact normalizes feelings and reduces isolation
9. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note (Postpartum Depression Screen)

Symptoms/behaviors endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, frequent tearfulness
- Excessive self-blame/guilt regarding infant care
- Daily generalized anxiety, nocturnal worry, two recent panic-equivalent episodes
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia tied to ruminative worries
- Feeling "overwhelmed"/unable to cope with routine tasks most days
- Passive self-harm ideation without intent or plan (fleeting "drive away" and cutting images)

Pattern:
Persistent depressive and anxiety symptoms present throughout the day, worsening at night, with associated functional impairment in self-care and infant-care tasks.

Screening significance:
Responses consistent with probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; passive self-harm thoughts warrant immediate safety/risk assessment.

Risk factors highlighted:
– Uncontrolled depressive symptoms (sadness, anhedonia, guilt)
– Clinically significant anxiety/panic
– Insomnia
– Passive suicidal ideation → SAFETY FLAG
